transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-10 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~42 min | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Priya, Ethan, Ravi (Skyline)

Summary (auto): Weekly check-in focused on pilot economics, caching wins, batching tradeoffs, and an action plan to run a 24h throughput test.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we have about 45 minutes on the calendar, we'll kick off with a quick recap of changes from last week then dig into the tokens per dollar numbers and the caching stats, sound good?
[00:18] Priya: yep, that's perfect. we've been watching the dashboards this morning, thanks for the quick patch you pushed to prefix caching.
[00:23] Carlos: sure — quick note, the prefix caching change was intentionally conservative, we only cached top-k prefixes for two of the high-traffic routes to avoid cache churn.
[00:33] Ethan: and that helped right away, we saw warm hit-rate jump from like 18% to 46% on the customer-support route, which lowered average tokens generated per request.
[00:46] Ravi: although we've noticed some variability, the first request after a deployment still feels slow, like cold path 95th latency is high.
[00:58] Maya: yup that's expected — prefix cache helps steady-state but cold starts and model load still dominate some tails. that's where batching and pre-warming play.
[01:08] Priya: can you walk us through the tokens/sec per dollar change after the caching update? numbers looked better but want the exact delta.
[01:18] Carlos: absolutely. overall tokens/sec per dollar for the POC workload increased by about 28% after the cache change when we hold batch policy constant. I have a couple of caveats though — that's measured on our hosted cluster with mixed request interarrival times.
[01:31] Ethan: okay, so 28% is great, but what happened to latency percentiles? we can't degrade SLOs.
[01:39] Carlos: 50th percentile latency improved by about 12%, 90th stayed flat, 95th increased by ~6% on the routes where we bumped batch size later in the test. so you get cost-per-token wins but tail latency can move opposite.
[01:52] Priya: that's my worry — users notice 95th more. do you have per-route breakdowns?
[01:58] Carlos: yes, I uploaded a per-route sheet. the onboarding flow (short prompts) benefits most from prefix caching because the model stops early; the long-form summarization route doesn't see as much cache benefit and is more sensitive to batch size.
[02:12] Maya: quick interruption — we should call out that we tried two batch policies: conservative (max 8) and aggressive (max 24). the aggressive batch improved tokens/$ by another 18% but raised 95th by ~15% on the long route.
[02:26] Priya: hmm. can we do dynamic batch sizing by route? like keep onboarding small and allow summarization to batch larger?
[02:33] Carlos: yes, routing by route and model shard is supported. the tradeoff is you need more runtime configuration and slightly more operational overhead. we can push rule-based batching per endpoint.
[02:44] Ravi: also, on the infra side, aggressive batching leads to occasional queue buildup that spikes memory for our pods, so we saw a few OOM warnings in staging.
[02:56] Ethan: did you try quantized model variant as well? we mentioned int8 last week.
[03:02] Carlos: we did a short test with an int8-quantized variant. throughput per GPU improved about 35% on average and cost-per-token drops materially, but there are occasional token-level quality regressions on rare tokens in the summarization route.
[03:19] Priya: I'd take the cost improvement if the quality delta is negligible for the majority of queries; can you give failure examples?
[03:26] Carlos: sure — we saw tokenization discrepancies and a couple of hallucinated dates in two of a thousand evaluation prompts. not a dealbreaker, but needs gating in production.
[03:36] Maya: suggested mitigation: use quantized variant for non-critical routes (internal summarization, batching-friendly) and keep float16 for customer-facing critical flows.
[03:45] Priya: ok that seems reasonable. back to caching — do you have the breakdown of absolute savings in token count?
[03:50] Carlos: yes. for the support route, prefix caching reduced generated tokens per session from median 420 to 210. net token spend dropped roughly 48% per session on warm hits. aggregated across all routes it's ~21% token reduction.
[04:07] Ethan: and how does that translate to dollars? we want tokens per dollar at the route level.
[04:12] Carlos: in the updated spreadsheet, support route tokens/dollar moved from 1.2k tokens/$ to about 1.8k tokens/$ with conservative batching. with aggressive batching and quantized model it reached close to 2.6k tokens/$.
[04:26] Priya: those are significant. what's the blended tokens/$ for our entire pilot traffic?
[04:31] Carlos: blended moved from ~1.05k/$ to ~1.35k/$ after caching, and with a mixed config (quantized on non-critical routes + selective aggressive batching) we project ~1.9k/$ but that's an extrapolation with several assumptions.
[04:45] Maya: note that projections assume sustained warm hit-rates and no sudden traffic spikes which would lower cache effectiveness.
[04:53] Ravi: any ideas on increasing cache hit-rate for the long-form route? it's low due to high prompt variability.
[04:59] Carlos: one approach is prompt canonicalization — normalize timestamps and variable identifiers before sending to model to increase reuse. we can add a lightweight preprocessor in front of the API.
[05:09] Priya: we've been hesitant about canonicalization because we worry about removing signals. but maybe for some flows it's safe. we'll run a quick eval.
[05:17] Ethan: security question — if we do stronger caching, how's PII handled? we can't cache sensitive payloads.
[05:23] Maya: good callout — Redwood's caching respects route-level flags. you can mark routes as non-cacheable, and we also support token redaction hooks and KMS integration for encrypted KV cache. we'll include the security doc in the drop.
[05:36] Priya: please do. also, can we get an audit of cached keys and a TTL policy recommendation?
[05:41] Carlos: yes, the recommendation is short TTL (30s-5m) for high-variance routes, longer (30m-6h) for stable dialogues. we'll send our suggested defaults and the live dashboard link.
[05:54] Maya: quick pivot to cost math — Priya asked earlier for a workback on the economics to the unit level. I ran a simple back-of-envelope: with current pilot capacity and average request mix, we estimate monthly token spend of $X (redacted in recording) but on projected optimized config that drops ~35%. full details in the spreadsheet.
[06:14] Priya: can you share the spreadsheet now?
[06:17] Carlos: yes link is in the meeting chat — "skyline_pilot_benchmarks_v3.xlsx". it has per-route sheets, assumptions, and the cost workback.
[06:25] Ravi: scanning it now, I see we need to validate the request trace used — our production mixes have a larger tail of long-form jobs. if you used a more average sample that could skew the blended number.
[06:37] Carlos: fair — we used production-ish test traces but we'll re-run with your weekly traffic capturing to be conservative. that's part of the 24h steady-state test.
[06:46] Priya: what's the plan for the 24h run— peak/backoff profile? we want realistic diurnal patterns.
[06:52] Maya: Carlos prepared a load script that can replay your real request traces or generate a diurnal synthetic. recommended: replay an anonymized week slice compressed into 24h using your privacy-safe trace. we'll provide the runbook.
[07:05] Ethan: on the infra side, for that 24h run we need VPC peering at scale and sustained egress throughput — can Redwood confirm network requirements?
[07:12] Carlos: yes, we documented the egress and peering guidance. for the aggressive batching tests you'll want headroom for larger in-flight requests; we'll include suggested instance sizing and GPU pool config.
[07:24] Priya: also a governance question — if we move some traffic to quantized variants, how will we monitor quality regressions?
[07:31] Carlos: we recommend running a shadow/compare mode for a subset of traffic (5-10%) and compute quick eval metrics — perplexity-ish proxies plus a small human eval sample daily. we can wire that into your monitoring alerts.
[07:44] Priya: that sounds good. can Redwood run the A/B and provide the delta dashboard?
[07:48] Carlos: yes, we can dashboard the diff and set regression thresholds.
[07:52] Maya: all right, next — pricing and commitment question surfaced: if we commit to a Dedicated pool for predictable throughput, does Redwood offer better unit economics vs hosted?
[08:01] Maya: (continuing) short answer: yes, committed Dedicated capacity lowers per-token platform fee and gives more predictable throughput; our pricing team can model that if you give target sustained RPS and latency SLOs.
[08:14] Priya: we'll need a workback. can you model a 99th percentile <500ms with 24/7 3k requests/day?
[08:23] Maya: we'll produce a Dedicated vs Hosted comparison showing per-token and per-hour costs and include SLA language. add to the deliverables.
[08:31] Ravi: one more technical item — cache persistence across deployments. currently, when we deploy new model versions we observed cache miss storms. any mitigation?
[08:40] Carlos: you can use cache warming strategies and causal-compatibility keys; also we support KV cache migration tools across model variants when the output tokenization is stable. it's a bit of engineering work but doable.
[08:52] Ethan: cool.
[08:55] Priya: action items recap?
[08:58] Maya: yes quick recap: Redwood shares updated benchmark spreadsheet and cost model (Maya), Redwood provides load script and runbook (Carlos), Skyline runs 24h run and shares logs (Ethan/Ravi), Priya to confirm exec time for results meeting.
[09:15] Priya: perfect. minor thing — can you also include a short doc on recommended TTL and canonicalization rules so we can review with our compliance folks?
[09:23] Carlos: will do, I'll include canonicalization examples and caution notes.
[09:28] Maya: great. anything else before we close?
[09:31] Priya: no, that's it — thanks.
[09:34] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links and the spreadsheet. bye.
